According to the letter, to qualify for severance, employees must remain active until their last scheduled day of work.

items.title: [discovermagazine.com] Study dates Taung Child to 3 million years, questions fossil classification
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A new study dates the Taung Child, a South African hominin fossil, to between 2.96 million and 3.03 million years ago—older than a previous estimate of 2.58 million—and argues that fossils long grouped as Australopithecus africanus may represent more than one species. Researchers compared tooth and brain development and found differences between the Taung Child and other fossils from the region. The team hypothesizes that repeated shifts between wet and dry climates changed habitats, sometimes isolating hominin populations and sometimes bringing them into contact. Fossilized pollen indicates the Taung Child lived in a wetter, more wooded setting than the area’s present-day landscape.

items.title: [phys.org] Researchers document sustained sexual bond between Ethiopian bull and male donkey
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An Italian-led research team documented repeated sexual interactions between a bull and a male donkey on an Ethiopian plateau, describing a selective social bond between the animals. During eight days of observation in March 2026, the bull, Achilles, mounted the donkey, Patroclus, 51 times; 34 mountings involved penetration. The findings appeared Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology. The pair also licked, rubbed and nuzzled one another, and researchers repeatedly saw them seek each other out despite access to other potential mates. The team cautions that observations of one domesticated pair cannot establish why the behavior occurred or what the animals felt. Dry-season conditions led herders to move them to separate pastures; researchers in Ethiopia are trying to arrange a reunion to observe whether their interactions resume.

items.title: [sci.news] Peruvian fossil reveals pygmy sperm whale with extreme skull asymmetry
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose fossil skull shows the most extreme facial asymmetry documented in a cetacean, and possibly in any mammal. The animal lived in what is now southern Peru between 6.3 million and 5.6 million years ago and was about 2.7 meters long. Both bony nostrils sat on the left side of its skull. Its dense, downward-curving snout and flexible neck suggest it searched for food in shallow seabed sediments. Researchers propose that it used echolocation to locate buried prey; unlike some bottom-feeding marine mammals, it had no facial whiskers or other specialized sensory structures for foraging.

items.title: [astronomy.com] Mars orbiter finds volcanic gas near Alba Mons, hinting magma persists
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers report that the European-Russian Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrogen chloride gas near Alba Mons on Mars during the planet’s cold aphelion season, when the gas is usually absent. The localized, out-of-season signal may come from magma releasing gas through fractures, suggesting that parts of Mars could remain volcanically active. The finding does not establish that an eruption is occurring. The team used observations from the orbiter’s Atmospheric Chemistry Suite and examined images of the region for possible pathways from underground. The study, published in Science Advances on Nov. 4, reports newly identified narrow fissures that could connect the gas to magmatic sources. Researchers say further observations, including attempts to detect sulfur dioxide from Earth, could help test the volcanic explanation.

items.title: [space.com] Hidden planet’s gravity tilts hot Jupiter out of view
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers say an unseen companion’s gravity tilted the orbit of TOI-2535 b, a hot Jupiter about 1,000 light-years away, until the planet stopped transiting its star in 2026. The UCLA-led team tracked the system with NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) from April 2019 to March 2026; the timing of the planet’s transits varied by as much as six hours before the crossings disappeared from view. The planet remains in the system, but its orbit is no longer aligned for telescopes observing from Earth to detect those crossings. The researchers estimate that TOI-2535 b may not transit again for 30 to 50 years, while the unseen companion could become observable sooner. Team members say the companion makes gradual inward migration a more likely explanation for the hot Jupiter’s close orbit than violent orbital scattering. The study appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters on Nov. 9.

items.title: [eos.org] Arctic ice cores trace century-old toxic pollution to Montana mine
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers traced arsenic and other heavy metals preserved in 10 Arctic ice cores to the Anaconda Copper Mine in Montana, linking pollution to a single industrial source thousands of kilometers away. Arsenic levels in some cores reached about 15 times preindustrial levels around 1914, according to the study in Nature Sustainability. By combining ice-core measurements, atmospheric modeling and historical production records, the team estimated that about 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic levels associated with increased health risks between 1898 and 1918. Pollution-control equipment installed at the smelter in 1919 reduced emissions by roughly 60% to 65%, though the mine continued operating until 1947. Lead researcher Joseph McConnell, a climate and environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, said epidemiologists should investigate the pollution’s potential effects on people.

items.title: [carbonbrief.org] El Niño-linked fires lift total carbon emissions despite fossil fuel dip
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

El Niño-related peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia are projected to push land-use carbon emissions higher in 2026, bringing total global CO₂ emissions to 43.3 billion tonnes even as fossil-fuel emissions edge down, according to the Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment. The researchers link the rise in land-use emissions to drier conditions and fires often ignited by human activity. The 21st Global Carbon Budget, published Nov. 10 in Earth System Science Data and presented during the U.N. climate conference in Antalya, projects 5.1 billion tonnes of emissions from land-use change this year. The projected decline in fossil-fuel emissions is partly attributable to the Iran conflict’s energy shock, alongside the growing contribution of solar, wind and electric vehicles. The report says the land carbon sink recovered in 2025 after weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño, but the strong 2026 El Niño is expected to weaken it again in 2027. Separately, an analysis of Chinese data found that emissions fell 3.1% in July-September, the country’s steepest quarterly drop since pandemic lockdowns in 2022.

A study by Katariina Nykyri, an Embry-Riddle researcher, proposes that millions of small plasma whirlpools on the Sun’s surface could help heat its much hotter corona. The study estimates that each vortex holds about two septillion ergs of energy. The study proposes that the vortices squeeze magnetic field lines until they reconnect, releasing energy as heat and fast-moving plasma. Separately, Earth-facing sunspot region AR4566 produced 18 of the Sun’s 19 flares in the 24 hours ending Nov. 10, all of them C-class. Forecasters said M-class flares remained possible through Nov. 11.

items.content_html:

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere and burned up over North Sumatra on Nov. 4, ending a nearly 22-year mission. Its observations, including millions of images, remain available for research. A 24-hour ultraviolet exposure of the Andromeda galaxy was assembled from observations made between May and July 2008. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

The agency warns that heat, drought and heavy rain can increase risks of heat illness, food insecurity and infectious disease, with vulnerable and conflict-affected communities facing particular danger. The WMO says the event is on track to reach record strength by December; its climate update uses data through September and does not include the latest impacts.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN warns climate adaptation funding leaves vulnerable countries exposed
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report says developing countries remain exposed to worsening floods, droughts and heat because adaptation funding is not reaching vulnerable communities at the scale required. Least-developed countries and small island states need an estimated $40 billion to $50 billion annually, equivalent to 3% to 4% of their gross domestic product, while support to least-developed countries fell 16% from 2022 to 2024. Adaptation measures include flood barriers, heat-resistant hospitals and drought-resilient water and farming systems. Low- and middle-income countries accounted for 99% of the 765 million people affected by floods and landslides between 2020 and 2025. Communities also face obstacles to turning plans into projects, including weak institutional coordination and difficulty accessing funding for climate-related losses. At the COP31 climate conference, opening in Antalya on Nov. 9, campaigners are urging governments to set out a concrete funding plan and prioritize grants or concessional loans over high-interest borrowing for projects that generate little direct revenue. Concessional loans are easier to repay than high-interest loans.

items.content_html:

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

items.title: [efeagro.com] Hackers raise supermarket freezer temperatures across Europe, spoiling food
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration at grocery stores and other businesses in several European countries overnight into Nov. 2, raising temperatures in some units to 50°C and prompting businesses to discard food or remove it as a precaution. Affected countries included Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg; reports also described incidents in Italy, though the extent there remains unclear. In Belgium, Delhaize reported refrigeration problems in about 40 stores, Carrefour in 15 and Spar in five. Ireland’s SuperValu reported incidents at 13 stores, while refrigeration supplier Danfoss said at least 17 Dutch businesses were affected. The attackers appear to have remotely changed settings on connected equipment, in some cases activating defrost mode. European Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described the repeated attacks as an attempt to disrupt food supply and weaken consumer trust, but said food security was not currently threatened. items.title: [cisa.gov] U.S. agencies warn hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration controls
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Five U.S. agencies warned on Nov. 5 that hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide, including controllers used by grocery stores, hospitals, food producers and transport operators. Attackers may exploit unpatched or internet-accessible devices to change temperatures or defrost settings, or prevent operators from seeing temperature readings. Such attacks could spoil stock, compromise storage safety and damage equipment. The warning follows attacks on European supermarkets on Nov. 2 and an incident that altered refrigeration settings at three French blood-service facilities. The U.S. agencies did not say whether refrigeration systems in the United States had been targeted. They urged operators to remove unnecessary internet access, secure remote connections, update firmware, isolate control systems from business networks and set alerts for unsafe temperature changes.

items.title: [bleepingcomputer.com] Russian Turla spies use Cereal malware to harvest government emails
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

ESET researchers say the Russian state-aligned cyberespionage group Turla used a previously undocumented toolkit called Cereal to spy on Microsoft Exchange servers at government organizations in Kazakhstan and Romania in late 2025. In Romania, the malware selectively collected messages involving European Union and NATO addresses. Cereal injects an email-collection component into Exchange’s transport process without interrupting normal mail delivery. The compromised server also receives commands, and researchers found no separate attacker-controlled command server. ESET says the toolkit can leave few traces on disk, but how Turla gained access to the servers remains unknown.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, flipping Senate seats in states including Texas, Ohio, Kansas and South Carolina. With 228 House seats and 54 Senate seats reported for the party, Democrats will control committees and confirmation votes when the new Congress convenes in January. President Donald Trump retains the power to veto legislation and direct executive policy. Voters’ concerns about living costs, inflation, tariffs and the Iran war contributed to Republican losses. The conflict, launched in February, drove fuel prices higher; U.S. inflation stood at 3.7% before the election. Markets initially wavered, then rallied on Nov. 4: the Dow rose 3%, while Brent crude fell 8.7% to $94.62 a barrel as investors reassessed the risk of prolonged conflict and political uncertainty. The new Congress also faces a Dec. 11 deadline to authorize government spending. Analysts expect legislative gridlock, and Trump may retain his executive authority to impose tariffs.
